Tiwanaku (Tiahuanaco) is the ruin of one of the most mysterious cities in the Andes. Debate about its purpose continues to this day. Here you can see the famous and distinctive Gateway of the Sun, the Akapana Pyramid, the "standing stones" of Kalasasaya and many other traces of an ancient culture.

During a tour, you can also admire blue lakes and ice caves where temperatures remain below freezing despite the proximity of the equator. You can journey through the "Valley of Spirits," take in the snow-covered peaks of the Illimani and Murata volcanoes, or admire the play of blue shades across the Cerro Zorro glacier.

Tiwanaku is an ancient city and the spiritual and political center of the Andean civilization of the same name. It has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2000. The city was first described in the Chronicles of Peru by Spanish historian Pedro Cieza de León.

At the southernmost tip of Argentina, on the island of Tierra del Fuego, mountains meet the sea, dense forests descend to the shores of cold bays, and the silence is broken only by the wind and the calls of seabirds. Tierra del Fuego National Park is one of Patagonia's most scenic places and Argentina's southernmost protected natural area.

The park lies near Ushuaia and occupies a stretch of coastline along the Beagle Channel. Its landscape is remarkably varied: forested mountains alternate with deep valleys, peat bogs, lakes, rivers and rocky seashores. The coves and bays are especially beautiful, with calm waters reflecting the outlines of the surrounding mountains.

Southern beech trees, characteristic of Patagonian forests, predominate in the woodlands. Walking trails pass among them, allowing visitors to experience Tierra del Fuego's natural surroundings from different perspectives. Some paths lead to mountain lakes and viewpoints, while others follow the coast, opening up views of islands, bays and the Beagle Channel.

The park's wildlife is also closely linked to its marine and forest environments. Numerous birds can be observed along the coast, while guanacos, foxes and other representatives of Patagonian fauna inhabit the forests and valleys. Marine mammals can be found in the coastal waters, and traveling along the channel brings a sense of the nearby, rugged Southern Ocean.

Lapataya Bay has a special place in the park as the final point of the famous Pan-American Highway route, which stretches across the Americas from Alaska to the southernmost part of the continent. Reaching it, travelers literally arrive at the end of the road and one of South America's most remote corners.

Tierra del Fuego captivates visitors through the completeness of its landscape rather than any single landmark. In one day, you can see mountains and forests, walk along the seashore, stop beside a quiet lake and experience the distinctive atmosphere of this distant southern land.

Tierra del Fuego National Park is a journey to the end of the world, where Patagonia's unspoiled nature reveals its diversity and the harsh climate only accentuates the beauty of this remarkable region.

On a trip from Buenos Aires, a walk around the town is complemented by a boat excursion through the delta. From the water, you can see green riverbanks, piers and houses beside the channels. Tigre is often visited together with the capital's northern suburbs, including San Isidro.

Tijuca is a national park within Rio de Janeiro. Forested hillsides, waterfalls and viewpoints sit alongside urban neighborhoods. It can be included in a Rio itinerary as a separate nature excursion.

The Floresta, Serra da Carioca and Pedra Bonita / Pedra da Gávea sectors are open to visitors. The forest sector has walking and picnic routes, while Serra da Carioca is home to Corcovado and the Christ the Redeemer statue. The experiences offered by the different sectors range from forest walks to mountain trails.

One of the waterfalls in the forest sector is Cascatinha Taunay. It can be seen near the main entrance to the Floresta sector. Around the waterfalls, the combination of water, rock and dense greenery is especially striking.

Tijuca remains a protected natural area. Visitors should stay on the trails, avoid feeding animals and refrain from collecting plants. A specific sector and route are chosen for an excursion; a single walk is not intended to cover the entire park.
